title: Sikh Dharma in the West
hookLine: Western converts since the 1970s, often in white turbans

lines: A WHITE TURBAN LEADS THE KIRTAN.
cards: A gurdwara in New Mexico, or California, or Massachusetts. A woman in a white turban leads the kirtan, and her Gurmukhi is careful and clear. Her parents were not Sikhs.

Neither were the parents of the man beside her on the tabla, who took a Sikh name as an adult. After the program, they serve langar alongside Punjabi families whose grandparents came from villages near Amritsar.
Everyone sits in the same rows. It's the story of a stream that flows far from Punjab.

teach.b: Sikh Dharma is the name used by a community of Sikhs in the West, among them people who came to the faith as adults. They first met it through a teacher of yoga and meditation from Punjab, known as Yogi Bhajan.

teach.h: THE REHAT TAKEN UP AS ADULTS.
teach.b: His students took up the rehat: uncut hair, the turban, the daily banis, often an early morning practice before dawn. Women in this community commonly wear the turban too, and white clothing is a familiar sight.
Two things need saying plainly. First, Sikhs have held differing views about this community: about the yoga it taught alongside Sikh practice, and about how its customs sit beside the Rehat Maryada.

Second, its founder's legacy is now seriously contested. Former students have come forward with grave accusations against him, and the community has had to face them, with members responding in different ways.

That is part of the story, and this path won't smooth it over. If this touches something in your own life, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
And yet the newcomers stand on something older than any teacher.
Guru Arjan, in Raag Dhanasari on Ang 671, sings, in paraphrase: I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to everyone.
A gurdwara with open doors and one row at langar was built for this: a stranger walks in, covers their head, sits down, and is fed.

This week brought the Taksal's careful reading, santhiaa, the Jatha's kirtan till dawn, Nanaksar's continuous praise, the Namdharis, Baba Dayal's reform, and now newcomers who learned the Guru's word as a second language.

how: Members of Sikh Dharma, a community of Sikhs in the West, keep the rehat and the daily banis, sing kirtan in Gurmukhi, and worship and serve langar alongside Punjabi Sikh families; women as well as men often wear the turban.

games.q: a newcomer walks into a gurdwara for the first time, unsure what to do. what does the gurdwara's design offer them?
o: a head covering, a seat, and food in the same row as everyone.
games.why: open doors and one row at langar: a stranger covers their head, sits down, and is fed.

practice: Bring to mind someone new in a place you know well, a coworker, a neighbor, someone who just joined a congregation, and remember being the new one, unsure where to sit.
Breathe in, picturing yourself showing them one small thing they'd need to know; breathe out, picturing them sitting down at ease.

wordCard.voice: Sikh Dharma in the West. A community of Sikhs in the West, among them people who took up the rehat as adults, often recognized by white dress and turbans worn by women and men. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: the Sikh faith, or the Sikh way.

carryVoice: Your line: newcomers welcome. One row at langar has room for whoever walks in. That's the week.
